transcript: The Cherry Orchard by Anton Chekhov is a strange play. Some may describe it as a comedy, others a tragedy. I'd call it a satirical allegory. When I saw the first preview of this production running at St. Ann's Warehouse, I was completely unfamiliar with it going in. There are a lot of characters, which initially concerned me, but over time I was able to form a solid understanding of who everyone is and what their relationships are. It basically revolves around an aristocratic family, their estate, and the people working there. The estate is home to the titular cherry orchard which is in danger of being auctioned off as the family faces mounting debts. A lot of the play is not very event-driven, so it can feel slow at times, and even when the dialogue is interesting, it's generally not riveting. But the slowness is somewhat amusing because the characters themselves have an air of boredom and passivity that's central to the point of this piece. Many of the characters are rather out of touch, indifferent, and dismissive. To me, this felt like The White Lotus in that it allows us to be a fly on the wall to some wildly out of touch people who will inevitably say some crazy stuff when left their own devices. But my interest in this vibe ran its course, and by part way through Act 2, I was pretty antsy waiting for something substantial to happen, which it eventually did. The finale, though drawn out, was very satisfying and creatively directed. Overall, I found this play to be interesting and at times very engaging, but I wouldn't expect to be “entertained” with a capital E, and the three hour run time didn't quite feel earned. With that, another program for my collection.
